nameStory: The hairy rubber cup gets its name from its unusual texture and appearance - when you touch it, it feels exactly like tough, rubbery gelatin rather than a typical mushroom. The 'hairy' part comes from its fuzzy, felt-like outer surface that looks like it's covered in tiny dark hairs. It's shaped like a cup or bowl, completing this peculiar trio of descriptive features.
description: The hairy rubber cup is a distinctive fungus that looks like someone carved a small bowl out of dark rubber and lined it with reddish-brown leather. Unlike typical mushrooms with caps and stems, this species forms cup-shaped fruit bodies that have an incredibly tough, gelatinous texture. The cups typically grow in small clusters and can range from about 1-3 inches across. What makes them truly unique is their rubber-like consistency - they're surprisingly tough and bouncy to the touch.

idTips.label: Rubbery texture
idTips.description: The most distinctive feature - press gently and it feels like firm rubber or tough jello, completely unlike any typical mushroom's soft or brittle texture

idTips.label: Cup shape
idTips.description: Forms distinct bowl or cup shapes, often slightly irregular, that hold their form even when handled

idTips.label: Two-toned coloring
idTips.description: Dark blackish-brown fuzzy exterior contrasts sharply with a smooth reddish-brown to rust-colored interior surface

idTips.label: Felt-like outer surface
idTips.description: The outside feels rough and velvety, like coarse felt fabric, with tiny hairs visible under close inspection

idTips.label: Grows on wood
idTips.description: Always found on decaying branches or partially buried wood, often in small clusters of 2-6 cups

idTips.label: Sturdy attachment
idTips.description: Firmly attached to its wood substrate - won't easily break off when gently tugged

habitat: Look for hairy rubber cups on decaying hardwood branches and logs in mixed and deciduous forests throughout New England's lower elevations. They particularly favor partially buried or well-rotted wood that's been decomposing for some time. You'll often find them in areas with rich, moist soil where fallen branches have been slowly breaking down.

seasonality.spring: Fresh fruit bodies begin appearing as the weather warms, often the best time to find perfect specimens with bright contrasting colors.
seasonality.summer: Peak fruiting season when clusters are most abundant and easy to spot on forest floors.
seasonality.fall: Still visible but may be weathered or past prime, though the rubbery texture helps them persist longer than softer fungi.
seasonality.winter: Old specimens may still be present but are usually dried out and less distinctive in appearance.

funFact: While North American field guides warn against eating this rubbery fungus, it's actually a popular food in Malaysia where people regularly harvest and cook it - proving that one culture's inedible curiosity can be another's dinner!
confusionNotes: Most cup fungi are thin and brittle, so the rubber-like texture immediately separates this from look-alikes. If you can press it and it bounces back like a rubber ball rather than crumbling or tearing, you've found your hairy rubber cup.
contextualKnowledge: Don't let the word 'cup' fool you into thinking this is delicate - these are some of the toughest fungi you'll encounter. The scientific name 'rufa' means reddish-brown, referring to the inner cup surface color.
compareHints: The hairy rubber cup is the only species in its genus Galiella found in New England, making it relatively easy to identify. Other cup fungi in the region are typically much more fragile and lack the distinctive rubbery texture. The closest relatives in the family Sarcosomataceae tend to be less gelatinous and don't have the characteristic felt-like exterior surface.
